messages.subject: using mlg.filter to produce a genclone object for mll
messages.subject_clean: using mlg.filter to produce a genclone object for mll
messages.body_plain:
Hi there, apologies if this has already been covered somewhere but I can't find much information on using the mlg.filter function. I have a dataset of 9k SNPs, no missing data but I suspect there might be clones in there.

I have two queries:

1. I don't quite understand how to determine the threshold to apply (I read about the cutoff_predictor function but have had little luck in actually using it)

2. When I've played around with arbitrary thresholds, I get a list assigning all samples to a given mll but how do I then convert this information to a genclone object to then do clone corrected analysis with?

Thanks in advance!

messages.subject_clean: [poppr] using mlg.filter to produce a genclone object for mll
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

> 1. I don't quite understand how to determine the threshold to apply (I read about the cutoff_predictor function but have had little luck in actually using it)

The choice of threshold is still a bit wobbly, I'm afraid. In short, you'll want to use the functions filter_stats() and cutoff_predictor(): https://grunwaldlab.github.io/poppr/reference/cutoff_predictor.html#examples

The best method is to look for an initial, small peak in the histogram of pairwise genetic distances and set the threshold to be between that peak and the larger peak (https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12550). The filter_stats() function will show you this histogram with an overlay of the number of multilocus lineages (MLL) present after a given threshold. The number of thresholds will always be the number of MLGs minus one. You can see that here: https://grunwaldlab.github.io/poppr/articles/mlg.html#tie-breakers-algorithms where there is a small peak that ends at a distance of ~0.11 that would collapse 71 MLG to 48 MLL.

The cutoff_predictor() function will take the threshold output of filter_stats() and try to find the largest gap between thresholds.

> 2. When I've played around with arbitrary thresholds, I get a list assigning all samples to a given mll but how do I then convert this information to a genclone object to then do clone corrected analysis with?

If you have your threshold chosen, you can apply to your genclone/snpclone object like so (assuming myData is the name of your object):

mlg.filter(myData) <- myThreshold + .Machine$double.eps^0.5

This is detailed in https://grunwaldlab.github.io/poppr/articles/mlg.html#filtered-contracted

So, if we were to follow the example of https://grunwaldlab.github.io/poppr/reference/cutoff_predictor.html#examples, we would use the results of cutoff_predictor() to set the threshold:

data(Pinf)
pinfreps <- fix_replen(Pinf, c(2, 2, 6, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 2))
pthresh  <- filter_stats(Pinf, distance = bruvo.dist, replen = pinfreps,
                         plot = TRUE, stats = "THRESHOLD", threads = 1L)

# prediction for farthest neighbor
cutoff_predictor(pthresh$farthest)
# [1] 0.1132221

mlg.filter(Pinf, dist = bruvo.dist, replen = pinfreps) <- cutoff_predictor(pthresh$farthest)
Pinf
#
# This is a genclone object
# -------------------------
# Genotype information:
#
#    48 contracted multilocus genotypes
#       (0.11) [t], (bruvo.dist) [d], (farthest) [a]
#    86 tetraploid individuals
#    11 codominant loci
#
# Population information:
#
#     2 strata - Continent, Country
#     2 populations defined - South America, North America

Hope that helps!
Zhian
-----
Zhian N. Kamvar, Ph. D.
Postdoctoral Researcher (Everhart Lab)
Department of Plant Pathology
University of Nebraska-Lincoln
ORCID: 0000-0003-1458-7108

messages.subject_clean: Confidence Intervals for poppr's other diversity statistics (e.g. Heterozygosity)
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I’d like to calculate confidence intervals for the expected and observed heterozygosity and I’m not sure if it’s possible to do that within poppr’s tools. Is this possible? I’d like to have output similar to what the diversity_ci function does for exp. heterozygosity. Is it possible to expand the stats that diversity_ci will calculate beyond the four that currently exist?

Thanks,

Karl

messages.subject: Re: [poppr] Confidence Intervals for poppr's other diversity statistics (e.g. Heterozygosity)
messages.subject_clean: [poppr] Confidence Intervals for poppr's other diversity statistics (e.g. Heterozygosity)
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Technically, expected and observed heterozygosity are calculated by adegenet (unless you are referring to the "Hexp" column in the poppr() function).

Unfortunately, diversity_ci() can only work for multilocus genotypes due to the differences between the type of data represented by multilocus genotype counts and alleles. However, you can roll-your-own with the shufflepop() function (assuming that you want to get an estimate of these values in a random-mating scenario). Here are the steps:

1. Generate 1000 simulations of your data from allele frequencies with shufflepop(method = 2)
2. Calculate expected and observed heterozygosity for each
3. Calculate the 5% and 95% quantiles.

Here's an example using data from a colony of cats in Nancy, France:

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library("poppr"))
data(nancycats)
nan9 <- nancycats[pop = 9]
het <- function(i){x <- summary(i);c(Hexp = mean(x$Hexp), Hobs = mean(x$Hobs))}
nan9samples <- replicate(1000, shufflepop(nan9, method = 2))
res <- sapply(nan9samples, het)
apply(res, 1, quantile, c(0.05, 0.95))
#>          Hexp      Hobs
#> 5%  0.5781893 0.5679012
#> 95% 0.6556927 0.7407407
het(nan9) # observed
#>      Hexp      Hobs
#> 0.6556927 0.7407407

Hope that helps,
Zhian

-----
Zhian N. Kamvar, Ph. D.
Postdoctoral Researcher (Everhart Lab)
Department of Plant Pathology
University of Nebraska-Lincoln
ORCID: 0000-0003-1458-7108

messages.subject: Re: [poppr] Identifying which pairs of individuals were clones in the data
messages.subject_clean: [poppr] Identifying which pairs of individuals were clones in the data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean,

You can use the `mlg.id <http://mlg.id>()` function to extract this information on the full (not clone-corrected) data set. It will return a list where each element represents a genotype and contains a vector of sample names. You can use this list to subset a data frame of geographic coordinates. See the example below.

library("poppr")
data(monpop)
show(monpop)
#>
#> This is a genclone object
#> -------------------------
#> Genotype information:
#>
#>    264 multilocus genotypes
#>    694 haploid individuals
#>     13 codominant loci
#>
#> Population information:
#>
#>      1 stratum - Pop
#>     12 populations defined -
#> 7_09_BB, 26_09_BB, 26_09_FR, ..., 45_10_FR, 26_11_BB, 26_11_FR
#
# Filter the data to collapse all genotypes that are different by
# at most one mutation
e <- .Machine$double.eps^0.5
mlg.filter(monpop) <- 1 + e
show(monpop)
#>
#> This is a genclone object
#> -------------------------
#> Genotype information:
#>
#>    190 contracted multilocus genotypes
#>        (1) [t], (diss.dist) [d], (farthest) [a]
#>    694 haploid individuals
#>     13 codominant loci
#>
#> Population information:
#>
#>      1 stratum - Pop
#>     12 populations defined -
#> 7_09_BB, 26_09_BB, 26_09_FR, ..., 45_10_FR, 26_11_BB, 26_11_FR
#
# The `mll()` function will list the multilocus genotype/lineage
# assignment per sample.

mll(monpop)[10:19] # Samples 10, 11, and 12 are all part of the same clone
#>  [1]  79  79  79  81 130  41  41  41  38 119

indNames(monpop)[10:19]
#>  [1] "A021" "A022" "A007" "A001" "A018" "A020" "A017" "A019" "A003" "A005"
#
# mlg.id <http://mlg.id> will identify them.
mlg.id <http://mlg.id>(monpop)[["79"]] # MLL 79 contains four clones
#> [1] "A021" "A022" "A007" "A033"
#
# Using this with a 2-column data frame of geographic coordinates
meandist <- function(i, df) mean(dist(df[i, , drop = FALSE]))
df  <- data.frame(x = rnorm(nInd(monpop)),
                  y = rnorm(nInd(monpop)),
                  row.names = indNames(monpop))
# Coordinates can be identified for MLL 79
ids <- mlg.id <http://mlg.id>(monpop)
df[ids[["79"]], , drop = FALSE]
#>               x          y
#> A021 -0.5901603 -0.5354590
#> A022 -1.2622871  0.9373863
#> A007  0.3141743 -1.3958612
#> A033 -1.5612730 -1.2284351
#
# loop over the list to calculate mean distance
res        <- vapply(mlg.id <http://mlg.id>(monpop), FUN = meandist, FUN.VALUE = numeric(1), df)
names(res) <- names(mlg.id <http://mlg.id>(monpop))
res[["79"]]
#> [1] 1.82423

> suppressPackageStartupMessages(library("poppr"))
> data(nancycats)
> nan9 <- nancycats[pop = 9]
> het <- function(i){x <- summary(i);c(Hexp = mean(x$Hexp), Hobs = mean(x$Hobs))}
> nan9samples <- replicate(1000, shufflepop(nan9, method = 2))
> res <- sapply(nan9samples, het)
> apply(res, 1, quantile, c(0.05, 0.95))
